Text: Java solves naming conflicts in large projects by using hierarchical {{c1::packages}} to partition the class namespace, and adopting the {{c2::reverse DNS}} naming convention to guarantee global uniqueness.
Extra: For example, `com.company.project` leverages the unique ownership of internet domains to ensure namespaces are isolated.

Text: The Java compiler enforces a physical mapping where dot-separated package name components correspond directly to {{c1::directory structures}}, enabling classloaders to translate a fully qualified name directly into a {{c2::filesystem path}}.
Extra: This layout ensures rapid, deterministic lookups relative to the classpath root, converting dots to directory slashes.

Text: While single-type imports load specific classes, {{c1::wildcard imports}} bring in all public classes of a package but are {{c2::non-recursive}}, meaning sub-packages must be imported separately.
Extra: Wildcard imports like `import java.util.*;` do not import sub-packages like `java.util.concurrent`.

Text: The keyword order must always be {{c1::import static}} instead of static import, and it is used to import static members directly into the local {{c2::file namespace}}.
Extra: This reduces class name qualification noise but increases the risk of naming collisions.

Text: If a source file has no package statement, it belongs to the unnamed {{c1::default package}}, from which classes {{c2::cannot be imported}} by classes in named packages.
Extra: This prevents named packages from developing compile-time dependencies on scratch files.

Text: To prevent conflicts on case-insensitive filesystems and with capitalized class names, Java package names must be written in {{c1::lowercase}}.
Extra: Filesystems like NTFS or APFS resolve paths regardless of case, making lowercase names critical for portability.

Text: Access visibility has four levels, where {{c1::package-private (default)}} access restricts access strictly to the same package and is active when no modifier is declared.
Extra: Package-private visibility helps developers hide internal package components from external library users.

Text: The traditional Classpath resolves classes via a flat {{c1::sequential search}}, which is susceptible to silent {{c2::package shadowing}} when multiple JARs contain duplicate class paths.
Extra: The JVM loads the first matching class it encounters on the classpath and discards the rest.

Text: Java 9 modules on the module path enforce strong encapsulation, blocking access to public classes unless their containing package is explicitly {{c1::exported}} in the module's {{c2::module-info.java}} file.
Extra: This replaces the permissive classpath model with strict boot-time validation of dependency constraints.
